data.claim: The printed pid is the setsid SESSION leader (a /bin/sh -c wrapper), not the review process; a plain kill <pid> stops only the wrapper and leaves the python review running.
data.falsifier: ps shows the reported pid comm is python3 (the review itself), or SIGTERM to the reported pid makes the twin-lock review pid exit.
data.mechanism: jobs.launch() reports the pid of "setsid /bin/sh -c ... &", which is the session+process-group leader; the review (sys.executable -m ddflow) is its child/subshell grandchild, so SIGTERM to the leader does not reach it. The review lock (twin.pid) records the review own os.getpid(), so the two pids differ.
data.probe: Ran jobs.launch() in /tmp/kilo with a python command that wrote os.getpid(); printed launch() return vs the command own pid, and ps -o pid,ppid,pgid,sid,comm.
data.probe_output: launch returned pid 2298257 (sh, pgid 2298257, sid 2298257); command own pid 2298258 (python3, ppid 2298257, pgid 2298257). CONFIRMED: the printed pid is the sh session leader, the review is a separate pid (2298258).
data.question: What pid does ddflow review --detach print, and does killing it stop the review?

evidence.note: Falsifiable claim CONFIRMED by running jobs.launch() in /tmp/kilo: returned pid 2298257 was the sh session leader (pgid/sid 2298257) while the review wrote os.getpid()=2298258. Recorded as research R62b5188d3f (CONFIRMED).

chunk_findings.detail: The last clause of previous finding 1 still holds: neither added test actually shows that `kill -- -2618834` reaches the still-running python review. Both tests only assert that the exact string `"kill -- -2618834"` is present in `_detach_note` output or in the dict handed to the fake `c.out`; no process group is created or signalled. The tests would still pass unchanged if the pid returned by `job_detach` were not the process group leader, or if the command string were emitted but still failed to signal the review. chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_detach.py:test_detach_note_names_a_stop_command_that_reaches_the_review and test_detach_emits_a_stop_command_in_the_prose_and_the_data

chunk_findings.detail: `_detach_stop` prints `kill -- -{pid}` and both new tests lock that string in (`kill -- -2618834`). Pasted into bash, the builtin does not treat `--` as end-of-options: `bash -c 'kill -- -2618834'` exits with `kill: --: invalid signal specification` and sends no signal. The setsid leader (2618834) and the python review (2618836) both stay alive, so the next review is still refused with "already being reviewed". A form bash actually accepts for a process-group kill is `kill -TERM -2618834` (or `command kill -- -2618834`); the printed recipe does not stop the review on the shell operators use.

chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_detach.py:test_detach_note_names_a_stop_command_that_reaches_the_review

chunk_findings.detail: Previous finding 1 is not fully answered: this new test still does not demonstrate that the stop command reaches a *non-leader* process. It spawns `setsid sleep 60`, so the only process in the new group is the leader itself. A defective `_detach_stop(pid)` that returned plain `kill -TERM <pid>` (the original bug shape: kills only the wrapper, leaves the python review alive) would make this test pass, because killing the sole group member is indistinguishable from killing the group. The test never creates a shell-wrapper leader plus a child review and asserts the child is gone, so it is still vacuous for `B-review-detach-prints-launcher-pid`; the other two tests only lock the exact `kill -TERM -<pid>` string.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_detach.py:test_detach_stop_command_stops_the_process_group

chunk_findings.detail: The new live test still does not show that the stop command reaches a child of the setsid leader, which is the failure in B-review-detach-prints-launcher-pid (wrapper 2618834 dies, python 2618836 keeps running). It only starts `setsid sleep 60`, so `leader.pid` is the sole member of the group; `bash -c 'kill -TERM -2618834'` and `bash -c 'kill -TERM 2618834'` both make `leader.returncode == -SIGTERM`. The two string tests only require the substring `"kill -TERM -2618834"` in `_detach_note` / `c.out`. None of the three tests fails if that command kills the launcher and leaves a same-group child alive.

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test still does not reproduce the original bug shape. It spawns `setsid sleep 60`, so the new process group contains only the leader. A defective `_detach_stop` that returned plain `kill -TERM <pid>` — killing only the leader and leaving a child review alive — would still make the test pass, because there is no second, non-leader process in the group. chunk_findings.detail: The test waits only for `childpid.exists()` before calling `int(childpid.read_text())`. The shell redirection `echo $! > '.../child.pid'` creates the file as empty before `echo` writes the PID, so under scheduling between the `open()`/truncate and the `write()` the test reads an empty string and raises `ValueError`. This makes the regression test flaky on a loaded runner.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_detach.py:test_detach_stop_command_kills_the_review_child_not_only_the_leader

chunk_findings.detail: After the group SIGTERM, the test only waits for `leader` via `leader.wait(timeout=5)` and then immediately asserts `_alive(review) is False`. Both leader and child receive the same group signal, but the leader can exit before the child; with no retry loop for the child to disappear, the assertion is a race and can spuriously fail if the review child is still alive/being reaped at that instant.
